title: Results
body_md:
Write $\bar\zeta:=q_0\zeta$ for the standardised explosion time.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,label=\textbf{\arabic*.}]
\item \textbf{Explosion criterion} (\cref{thm:dichotomy}). For every i.i.d.\ positive idea-size law in this model, explosion is almost sure if $r>1$ and impossible if $r\le1$. For equal sizes and a monotone rate function, explosion of the chain is equivalent to blow-up of its fluid equation.
\item \textbf{Exact timing law} (\cref{thm:law,thm:random,cor:gamma}). For equal sizes, $\bar\zeta$ has Laplace transform $1/(-s;q)_\infty$, moments $n!/(q;q)_n$, Mellin transform $\Gamma(1+s)(q^{1+s};q)_\infty/(q;q)_\infty$ and an alternating $q$-series distribution function. Its slow tail is $\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta>t)\sim e^{-t}\sum_mp(m)q^m$, and at fixed $q$ it has the two-term small-time asymptotic $\log\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta\le t)=-\frac{L^2}{2\ell}-\frac{L\log L}{\ell}+O(L)$, $L=\log(1/t)$. For random sizes $\bar\zeta$ is a perpetuity with explicit moments, and when $\log(1+H)$ is exponential (Lomax sizes), $\bar\zeta$ is exactly Gamma distributed. Most of these formulas are known (\cref{tab:contrib}); we give self-contained proofs.
\item \textbf{Residual-time self-similarity} (\cref{thm:selfsim,prop:logperiodic,prop:uncertain}). With parameters fixed and known, at every stopping time $\tau$ the remaining time $\zeta-\tau$, multiplied by the current idea rate, has the law of $\bar\zeta$, independent of the past. Relative predictive uncertainty therefore does not vanish as explosion approaches. In coordinates centred on the realised explosion time, the mean density of ideas is log-periodic with harmonics $\Gamma(1-2\pi ik/\ell)$. If the growth exponent is uncertain with positive density at the critical value, then $t\,\mathbb{P}(\zeta>t\mid\varepsilon>0)$ converges to an explicit constant.
\item \textbf{Fixed-sample detection} (\cref{thm:detect,cor:warning}). For the binary experiment with known baseline rate and known increment $\ell$, decided once after the first $n$ waiting times, the minimum sample size at level $\alpha$ satisfies $n^\ast\sim(12z_\alpha^2)^{1/3}\ell^{-2/3}$, with non-asymptotic bounds on both sides.
\item \textbf{Model extensions} (\cref{thm:lag,prop:diversion,thm:race}). In a deterministic delayed-feedback model any fixed delay $D>0$ prevents blow-up and gives $\log\log A(t)\sim t\log r/D$; the corresponding stochastic model does not explode. Power-law diversion of effort changes the explosion threshold. In a deterministic race with a fixed allocation share, the asymptotic regime of the oversight-to-capability ratio is determined by exponents, except at a critical equality where the allocation enters the limit.
\end{enumerate}

label: def:good
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:good}
Let $A_0>0$, $\kappa>0$, $\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $(0,\infty)$, the \emph{idea-size law}. Let $(e_n)_{n\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ and $(H_n)_{n\ge1}$ i.i.d.\ with law $\mu$, all independent. Put
\[
A^{(0)}:=A_0,\qquad A^{(n)}:=A^{(n-1)}(1+H_n),\qquad \tau_n:=\frac{e_n}{\kappa\,(A^{(n)})^{\varepsilon}},\qquad T_n:=\sum_{k<n}\tau_k,
\]
and $\zeta:=\lim_n T_n\in(0,\infty]$. The \emph{Good process} is $A_t:=A^{(n)}$ for $T_n\le t<T_{n+1}$, with $A_t:=\infty$ for $t\ge\zeta$. Its idea count is $N_t:=n$ on $[T_n,T_{n+1})$, $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ is the usual augmentation of the filtration generated by $(A_t)$, and $\zeta$ is its \emph{explosion time} ($\zeta=\infty$ means no explosion).
head: environment
name: Good process

label: rem:scope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:scope}
We study a tractable stochastic realisation of the feedback law \eqref{eq:ode}, not a unique stochastic model implied by that law. The assumptions of independent positive multiplicative improvements and exponential holding times make the clock explicit. Our robustness statements concern the specified family of processes; they do not establish robustness to arbitrary dependence, negative shocks, time-varying returns or alternative observation schemes. The assumptions are used as follows.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
\item Geometric rates together with exponential holding times produce the $q$-products of \cref{thm:law}.
\item The memoryless property of the holding times is what makes the residual-time statement of \cref{thm:selfsim} hold at \emph{arbitrary} stopping times, not just at idea times.
\item The explosion criterion of \cref{thm:dichotomy}\ref{it:dich-power} needs i.i.d.\ strictly positive sizes but no moment condition on $H$; matching a finite level drift through $\mathbb{E} H$ (\cref{box:calibration}, convention A) does need $\mathbb{E} H<\infty$.
\item What counts as one ``idea'' is a modelling choice. Grouping several exponential waiting stages into one idea generally produces a non-exponential holding time, so a coarser idea definition is not automatically another Good process.
\end{itemize}

label: rem:lamperti
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:lamperti}
Let $M$ be a unit-rate Poisson process independent of $(H_i)$, and let $\xi_s:=\sum_{i\le M_s}\log(1+H_i)$, a compound Poisson subordinator. Measure time in ``ideas'' $s$ and convert it to calendar time through $\,\mathrm{d} t=\,\mathrm{d} s/(\kappa A^{\varepsilon})$. Then $A_t=A_0\exp(\xi_{\sigma(t)})$, where $\sigma$ is the inverse of $s\mapsto(\kappa A_0^{\varepsilon})^{-1}\int_0^s e^{-\varepsilon\xi_u}\,\mathrm{d} u$, and
\[
\zeta=(\kappa A_0^{\varepsilon})^{-1}\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon\xi_s}\,\mathrm{d} s .
\]
Thus $A$ is a positive self-similar Markov process in the sense of Lamperti \cite{Lam72}, with a negative index: if $A$ starts at $a$, then $(cA_{c^{\varepsilon}t})_{t\ge0}$ has the law of $A$ started at $ca$. Moreover $\zeta$ is an \emph{exponential functional} of the subordinator $\varepsilon\xi$ \cite{CPY97,BY05}.

label: prop:fluid
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:fluid}
Consider the lattice case with $\kappa=c/h$ (convention A) for fixed $c>0$, $\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$ and $A_0>0$. For $a>A_0$ let $T^h(a):=\inf\{t:A_t\ge a\}$ and $t(a):=\int_{A_0}^a \,\mathrm{d} x/(cx^{1+\varepsilon})$, the time the solution of \eqref{eq:ode} takes to reach $a$. Then $T^h(a)\to t(a)$ in $L^2$ as $h\downarrow0$. If $\varepsilon>0$, then also $\zeta^h\to T^\ast=(\varepsilon cA_0^{\varepsilon})^{-1}$ in $L^2$.
head: environment
name: Fluid limit of hitting times

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x_k:=A_0(1+h)^k$ and $n:=\min\{k:x_k\ge a\}$, so that $T^h(a)=T_n=\sum_{k<n}e_k/q_k$ with $q_k=c\,x_k^{\varepsilon}/h$. Since $x_{k+1}-x_k=hx_k$,
\[
\mathbb{E} T_n=\sum_{k<n}\frac{h}{c\,x_k^{\varepsilon}}=\sum_{k<n}\frac{x_{k+1}-x_k}{c\,x_k^{1+\varepsilon}}
\]
is a Riemann sum for $\int_{A_0}^{x_n}\,\mathrm{d} x/(cx^{1+\varepsilon})$ with mesh at most $ha(1+h)$. Since $x_n\in[a,a(1+h))$, we get $\mathbb{E} T_n\to t(a)$. Moreover $\operatorname{Var} T_n=\sum_{k<n}q_k^{-2}\le(\max_{k<n}q_k^{-1})\,\mathbb{E} T_n$, and $\max_{k<n}q_k^{-1}\le h\max(A_0^{-\varepsilon},a^{-\varepsilon})/c\to0$. Hence $\mathbb{E}|T_n-t(a)|^2=\operatorname{Var} T_n+(\mathbb{E} T_n-t(a))^2\to0$. For $\varepsilon>0$, \eqref{eq:zeta} gives
\[
\mathbb{E}\zeta^h=\frac{h}{cA_0^{\varepsilon}(1-(1+h)^{-\varepsilon})}\to\frac1{\varepsilon cA_0^\varepsilon},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}\zeta^h=\frac{h^2}{c^2A_0^{2\varepsilon}(1-(1+h)^{-2\varepsilon})}\to0. \qedhere
\]

label: thm:dichotomy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:dichotomy}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item\label{it:dich-general} \emph{Lattice sizes, arbitrary rates.} Let $h>0$, let $\nu:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be any function, and consider the pure birth chain with rates $q_n=\nu(A_0(1+h)^n)$, i.e.\ the lattice process with rate function $\nu$ in place of $\kappa a^{\varepsilon}$. Then $\mathbb{P}(\zeta<\infty)=1$ if $\sum_n 1/q_n<\infty$, and $\mathbb{P}(\zeta=\infty)=1$ otherwise. If $\nu$ is monotone, then $\sum_n1/q_n<\infty$ if and only if
\[
\int_{A_0}^\infty\frac{\,\mathrm{d} x}{x\,\nu(x)}<\infty,
\]
which is the Osgood condition for finite-time blow-up of the fluid equation $\dot a=h\,a\,\nu(a)$.
\item\label{it:dich-power} \emph{Power rates, arbitrary sizes.} For the Good process with any i.i.d.\ strictly positive idea-size law $\mu$: if $\varepsilon>0$ then $\mathbb{E}[\zeta^m]<\infty$ for every $m\ge1$, so in particular $\zeta<\infty$ a.s.; if $\varepsilon\le0$ then $\zeta=\infty$ a.s. No moment condition on $\mu$ is needed.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Explosion criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{it:dich-general} Here $\zeta=\sum_n e_n/q_n$ with deterministic $q_n$. If $\sum 1/q_n<\infty$ then $\mathbb{E}\zeta<\infty$. If $\sum 1/q_n=\infty$, then $\sum_n\log(1+1/q_n)=\infty$ (use $\log(1+x)\ge x/2$ for $x\le1$), so $\mathbb{E} e^{-\zeta}=\prod_n(1+1/q_n)^{-1}=0$ and $\zeta=\infty$ a.s. For the integral test, suppose $\nu$ is nondecreasing. Then $u\mapsto1/\nu(A_0(1+h)^u)$ is nonincreasing, so its sum over $u\in\mathbb{N}$ and its integral over $[0,\infty)$ converge together. The substitution $x=A_0(1+h)^u$ turns the integral into $(\log(1+h))^{-1}\int_{A_0}^\infty\,\mathrm{d} x/(x\nu(x))$. If $\nu$ is nonincreasing, both the sum and the integral diverge.

\ref{it:dich-power} Let $Y_i:=(1+H_i)^{-\varepsilon}$. Then $\bar\zeta:=\kappa A_0^\varepsilon\zeta=\sum_n e_n\prod_{i\le n}Y_i$. If $\varepsilon>0$, then $Y_i\in(0,1)$ a.s., so $y_m:=\mathbb{E} Y^m<1$ for every $m$. By Minkowski's inequality in $L^m$ and independence,
\[
\|\bar\zeta\|_m\le\sum_{n\ge0}\|e_n\|_m\Big\|\prod_{i\le n}Y_i\Big\|_m=(m!)^{1/m}\sum_{n\ge0}y_m^{n/m}<\infty .
\]
If $\varepsilon\le0$, then $Y_i\ge1$ and $\bar\zeta\ge\sum_ne_n=\infty$ a.s.

label: cor:threshold
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:threshold}
In the parametrisation of \eqref{eq:ode}, with $\beta>0$, a Good process explodes almost surely if $r>1$ and never explodes if $r\le1$, for every i.i.d.\ strictly positive idea-size law and every $\kappa$. Within this model, randomness changes when the explosion happens, but not whether it does.
head: environment
name: The threshold is $r=1$

label: rem:saturation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:saturation}
Part \ref{it:dich-general} also covers the working paper's observation that $r$ must eventually fall below $1$ because of physical limits \cite[note~5]{CASP26}. Any monotone rate function with $\int^\infty\,\mathrm{d} x/(x\nu(x))=\infty$, for example one that saturates, prevents explosion almost surely. The singularity is a property of the idealised power law.

label: thm:law
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:law}
Let $q\in(0,1)$, $\ell=\log(1/q)$, and $\bar\zeta=\sum_{n\ge0}e_nq^n$ as in \eqref{eq:zeta}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item\label{it:laplace} \emph{Laplace transform.} $\mathbb{E} e^{-s\bar\zeta}=1/(-s;q)_\infty$ for $s>-1$.
\item\label{it:moments} \emph{Moments count partitions.} For $n\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,n}=\frac{n!}{(q;q)_n},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \frac{\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,n}}{n!}=\sum_{m\ge0}p_{\le n}(m)\,q^m .
\]
\item\label{it:series} \emph{Distribution.} For $t\ge0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta>t)=\frac{1}{(q;q)_\infty}\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^kq^{k(k+1)/2}}{(q;q)_k}\,e^{-t/q^k},
\qquad
f_{\bar\zeta}(t)=\frac{1}{(q;q)_\infty}\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^kq^{k(k-1)/2}}{(q;q)_k}\,e^{-t/q^k}.
\]
\item\label{it:slow} \emph{Slow tail.} For $t\ge0$,
\[
\Big|\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta>t)-\mathcal P(q)\,e^{-t}\Big|\le\frac{(-q;q)_\infty}{(q;q)_\infty}\,e^{-t/q} .
\]
\item\label{it:fast} \emph{Small-time asymptotic.} At fixed $q$, as $t\downarrow0$, with $L:=\log(1/t)$,
\[
\log\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta\le t)=-\frac{L^2}{2\ell}-\frac{L\log L}{\ell}+O(L).
\]
\item\label{it:mellin} \emph{Mellin transform.} The function $s\mapsto\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,s}$ is entire, and for all $s\in\mathbb{C}$
\[
\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,s}=\frac{\Gamma(1+s)\,(q^{1+s};q)_\infty}{(q;q)_\infty},
\]
where the right-hand side has removable singularities at $s=-1,-2,\dots$. In particular, for $n\ge1$,
\[
\mathbb{E}\big[\bar\zeta^{-n}\big]=\frac{\ell}{(n-1)!}\prod_{m=1}^{n-1}(\rho^m-1),\qquad\text{so}\qquad \mathbb{E}[1/\bar\zeta]=\ell .
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Exact law, lattice case

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{it:laplace} By independence, $\mathbb{E} e^{-s\bar\zeta}=\prod_k\mathbb{E} e^{-sq^ke_k}=\prod_k(1+sq^k)^{-1}$ for $s>-1$.

\ref{it:moments} By \eqref{eq:euler1} with $z=-s$, $\mathbb{E} e^{-s\bar\zeta}=\sum_n(-s)^n/(q;q)_n$ for $|s|<1$. Since $\bar\zeta$ has exponential moments of small order, this expansion equals $\sum_n(-s)^n\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,n}/n!$. The partition statement is the expansion $\prod_{j=1}^n(1-q^j)^{-1}=\prod_{j=1}^n\sum_{a_j\ge0}q^{ja_j}$.

\ref{it:series} Let $\bar\zeta_n:=\sum_{k<n}e_kq^k$. Its summands are independent exponentials with distinct rates $q^{-k}$, so by the classical formula for the hypoexponential law,
\[
\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta_n>t)=\sum_{k<n}c^{(n)}_k e^{-t/q^k},\qquad c^{(n)}_k:=\prod_{\substack{j<n\\ j\neq k}}\frac{1}{1-q^{j-k}} .
\]
The factors with $j<k$ equal $(1-q^{-m})^{-1}=-q^m/(1-q^m)$ with $m=k-j\in\{1,\dots,k\}$, and those with $j>k$ equal $(1-q^m)^{-1}$ with $m=j-k\in\{1,\dots,n-1-k\}$. Hence
\[
c^{(n)}_k=\frac{(-1)^kq^{k(k+1)/2}}{(q;q)_k\,(q;q)_{n-1-k}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\frac{(-1)^kq^{k(k+1)/2}}{(q;q)_k\,(q;q)_\infty},
\]
and $|c^{(n)}_k|\le q^{k(k+1)/2}/(q;q)_\infty^2$, which is summable. Since $\bar\zeta_n\uparrow\bar\zeta$, $\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta_n>t)\uparrow\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta>t)$, and dominated convergence gives the series. As a check, at $t=0$ the series equals $1$ by \eqref{eq:euler2} with $z=q$. Differentiating term by term gives the density; this is justified because, uniformly in $t\ge0$, the differentiated series is dominated by the convergent series $\sum_kq^{k(k-1)/2}/(q;q)_k$.

\ref{it:slow} The $k=0$ term of the series is $e^{-t}/(q;q)_\infty$. For $k\ge1$ we have $e^{-t/q^k}\le e^{-t/q}$, and by \eqref{eq:euler2} with $z=-q$,
\[
\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{q^{k(k+1)/2}}{(q;q)_k}\le(-q;q)_\infty .
\]
(Probabilistically, $\bar\zeta=e_0+X$ with $X$ independent of $e_0$ and $\mathbb{E} e^{X}=\prod_{k\ge1}(1-q^k)^{-1}=\mathcal P(q)$: a slow takeoff needs only a slow \emph{first} idea.)

\ref{it:fast} \emph{Upper bound.} For $s\ge1$ let $m:=\lfloor\log s/\ell\rfloor$ and write $\log s=\ell(m+\theta)$ with $\theta\in[0,1)$. Since $\log(1+x)\ge\log x$ and $sq^k\ge1$ for $k\le m$,
\[
\log(-s;q)_\infty\ \ge\ \sum_{k=0}^m(\log s-k\ell)=\ell(m+1)\Big(\frac m2+\theta\Big)\ \ge\ \frac{\ell(m+\theta)^2}{2}=\frac{(\log s)^2}{2\ell},
\]
because $(m+1)(m+2\theta)-(m+\theta)^2=m+2\theta-\theta^2\ge0$. By Chernoff's bound and \ref{it:laplace}, $\log\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta\le t)\le st-(\log s)^2/(2\ell)$. Choose $\log s=L+\log(L/\ell)$, which is admissible once $L\ge\ell$, so that $st=L/\ell$. Then
\[
\log\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta\le t)\le\frac L\ell-\frac{(L+\log(L/\ell))^2}{2\ell}\le-\frac{L^2}{2\ell}-\frac{L\log L}{\ell}+\frac{(1+\log\ell)L}{\ell}.
\]
\emph{Lower bound.} Let $n:=\lceil(L+\log\frac{4}{1-q})/\ell\rceil$. Let $E_1:=\{e_k\le x_k\ \forall k<n\}$ with $x_k:=tq^{-k}/(2n)$, and $E_2:=\{\sum_{k\ge n}e_kq^k\le t/2\}$. These events are independent and $E_1\cap E_2\subseteq\{\bar\zeta\le t\}$. By Markov's inequality, $\mathbb{P}(E_2^c)\le 2q^n/((1-q)t)\le\frac12$. Since $1-e^{-x}\ge\frac12\min(x,1)$,
\[
\log\mathbb{P}(E_1)\ge-n\log2+\sum_{k<n}\min(0,k\ell-M),\qquad M:=L+\log(2n).
\]
The function $k\mapsto M-k\ell$ is decreasing, so the sum over $0\le k\le M/\ell$ of $M-k\ell$ is at most $M+M^2/(2\ell)$. Hence
\[
\log\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta\le t)\ \ge\ -\log 2-n\log2-M-\frac{M^2}{2\ell}.
\]
Now $n=L/\ell+O(1)$ and $\log(2n)=\log L+O(1)$, so $M^2=L^2+2L\log L+O(L)$, and the lower bound matches the upper bound up to $O(L)$.

\ref{it:mellin} For $\Re s>-1$, integrate the density in \ref{it:series} against $t^s$ term by term, using
\[
\int_0^\infty t^se^{-t/q^k}\,\mathrm{d} t=\Gamma(1+s)\,q^{k(1+s)} .
\]
The interchange is justified by absolute convergence, since the series $\sum_k q^{k(k-1)/2+k(1+\Re s)}/(q;q)_k$ converges. Then
\[
\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,s}=\frac{\Gamma(1+s)}{(q;q)_\infty}\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^kq^{k(k-1)/2}(q^{1+s})^k}{(q;q)_k}=\frac{\Gamma(1+s)(q^{1+s};q)_\infty}{(q;q)_\infty}
\]
by \eqref{eq:euler2}. By \ref{it:fast} and \ref{it:slow}, $\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,x}<\infty$ for every real $x$. So $s\mapsto\mathbb{E} e^{s\log\bar\zeta}$ is the moment generating function of $\log\bar\zeta$, finite on all of $\mathbb{R}$, and therefore entire. On the right-hand side, the pole of $\Gamma(1+s)$ at $s=-n$ is cancelled by the zero of the factor $1-q^{s+n}$ in $(q^{1+s};q)_\infty$. The identity theorem extends the formula to $\mathbb{C}$. Near $s=-n$ we have $\Gamma(1+s)\sim(-1)^{n-1}/((n-1)!(s+n))$ and $1-q^{s+n}\sim\ell(s+n)$. The remaining factors give $\prod_{m=1}^{n-1}(1-q^{-m})\cdot(q;q)_\infty$, and combining these yields the stated negative moments.

label: cor:moments
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:moments}
$\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta=\dfrac1{1-q}$, $\operatorname{Var}\bar\zeta=\dfrac1{1-q^2}$, and $\operatorname{CV}(\bar\zeta)=\sqrt{\dfrac{1-q}{1+q}}$. As $q\uparrow1$ (small ideas), $\operatorname{CV}\sim\sqrt{\ell/2}\to0$, consistent with \cref{prop:fluid}. As $q\downarrow0$ (one giant idea), $\operatorname{CV}\to1$.

label: rem:casp-mean
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:casp-mean}
Chan et al.\ assume that each doubling of $A$ takes $2^{-\varepsilon}\approx0.76$ times as long as the previous one, starting from $4.5$ months, and sum nine terms of the geometric series \cite[SM]{CASP26}. For a Good process with doubling-sized ideas ($h=1$) under convention~B, $q_0=1/d_0$ and the expected duration of the $k$-th doubling is exactly $d_0q^k$ with $q=2^{-\varepsilon}$. So their seventeen months is, up to rounding, $\mathbb{E} T_9=17.3$ months, and the full series $d_0/(1-2^{-\varepsilon})=19.00$ months is $\mathbb{E}\zeta$. \Cref{thm:law} supplies the rest of the distribution (\cref{tab:law}).

head: environment
name: Random idea sizes

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) $\bar\zeta=e_0+Y_1\sum_{n\ge1}e_n\prod_{2\le i\le n}Y_i$, and the last sum is a copy of $\bar\zeta$ independent of $(e_0,Y_1)$. (b) All moments are finite by \cref{thm:dichotomy}\ref{it:dich-power}. Expanding $(e+Y\bar\zeta')^m$ and isolating the term $j=m$ gives
\[
(1-y_m)\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,m}=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\frac{m!}{j!}\,y_j\,\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,j}\qquad(y_0:=1).
\]
The claim follows by induction from the telescoping identity $\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}y_j\prod_{i=1}^j(1-y_i)^{-1}=\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}(1-y_i)^{-1}$; to verify it, add the term $j=m$ to both sides and use $(1-y_m)+y_m=1$. (c) follows from (b) with $m=1,2$.

label: cor:lattice-min
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:lattice-min}
Among all idea-size laws with the same standardised mean explosion time $\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta=1/(1-y_1)$ (equivalently, the same mean at a common current rate $\kappa A_0^{\varepsilon}$), the coefficient of variation of $\bar\zeta$ is minimised exactly when $Y$ is a.s.\ constant, i.e.\ in the lattice case.

name: Equal ideas are the most predictable

title: Proof
body_md: At fixed $y_1$, $\operatorname{CV}^2$ is increasing in $y_2$, and $y_2\ge y_1^2$, with equality if and only if $Y$ is a.s.\ constant.

label: cor:gamma
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:gamma}
Let $\varepsilon>0$, $b>0$, and suppose $\mathbb{P}(H>x)=(1+x)^{-b\varepsilon}$ for $x\ge0$; equivalently, $\log(1+H)$ is exponential with rate $b\varepsilon$, or $Y=(1+H)^{-\varepsilon}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(b,1)$. Then
\[
\bar\zeta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(b+1,1),\qquad \mathbb{E}\bar\zeta=b+1,\qquad \operatorname{CV}(\bar\zeta)=\frac1{\sqrt{b+1}} .
\]
At the same standardised mean the lattice case has $\operatorname{CV}=1/\sqrt{2b+1}$, in line with \cref{cor:lattice-min}. The improvement size has finite mean if and only if $b\varepsilon>1$; the corollary needs no such condition.
head: environment
name: Lomax ideas give a Gamma explosion time

title: Proof
body_md:
$\mathbb{P}(Y\le y)=\mathbb{P}\big(1+H\ge y^{-1/\varepsilon}\big)=y^{b}$, so $Y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(b,1)$ and $y_j=b/(b+j)$. By \cref{thm:random}(b),
\[
\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta^{\,m}=m!\prod_{j=1}^m\frac{b+j}{j}=\frac{\Gamma(b+m+1)}{\Gamma(b+1)} ,
\]
which are the moments of $\operatorname{Gamma}(b+1,1)$. The Gamma law is determined by its moments (its moment generating function is finite near $0$), so $\bar\zeta\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(b+1,1)$. As a direct check, $F(s)=(1+s)^{-(b+1)}$ satisfies the transform form of \cref{thm:random}(a), $F(s)=(1+s)^{-1}\mathbb{E} F(sY)$, because $\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d} y}\big[y^b(1+sy)^{-b}\big]=b\,y^{b-1}(1+sy)^{-b-1}$ gives $\int_0^1 b\,y^{b-1}(1+sy)^{-(b+1)}\,\mathrm{d} y=(1+s)^{-b}$. For the lattice comparison, $\mathbb{E}\bar\zeta=b+1$ forces $q=b/(b+1)$, and $(1-q)/(1+q)=1/(2b+1)$.

label: rem:ramanujan
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ramanujan}
For $0<u<1$, Tonelli's theorem applied to $\bar\zeta^{-u}=\Gamma(u)^{-1}\int_0^\infty s^{u-1}e^{-s\bar\zeta}\,\mathrm{d} s$, together with \cref{thm:law}\ref{it:laplace} and \ref{it:mellin} at $s=-u$, gives
\[
\int_0^\infty\frac{t^{u-1}\,\mathrm{d} t}{(-t;q)_\infty}=\frac{\pi}{\sin\pi u}\,\frac{(q^{1-u};q)_\infty}{(q;q)_\infty},
\]
an evaluation in the circle of Ramanujan's $q$-beta integrals \cite{Ask80,GR04}.
head: environment
name: A Ramanujan integral

label: thm:selfsim
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:selfsim}
In the lattice case with $\varepsilon>0$, let $\tau$ be any $(\mathcal{F}_t)$-stopping time. On $\{\tau<\zeta\}$, conditionally on $\mathcal{F}_\tau$, the random variable $q_{N_\tau}(\zeta-\tau)$ has law $\Lambda_q$. That is, for every bounded measurable $\varphi$,
\[
\mathbb{E}\big[\varphi\big(q_{N_\tau}(\zeta-\tau)\big)\mathbf 1_{\{\tau<\zeta\}}\,\big|\,\mathcal{F}_\tau\big]=\mathbf 1_{\{\tau<\zeta\}}\,\mathbb{E}\varphi(\bar\zeta),
\]
where expressions multiplied by $\mathbf 1_{\{\tau<\zeta\}}$ are read as zero outside that event.
head: environment
name: Residual-time self-similarity

title: Proof
body_md: $(N_t)$ is the minimal pure birth chain with rates $(q_n)$. By the strong Markov property of minimal continuous-time Markov chains \cite{Nor97}, on $\{\tau<\zeta,\ N_\tau=n\}$ and conditionally on $\mathcal{F}_\tau$, the process $(N_{\tau+s}-n)_{s\ge0}$ is a minimal pure birth chain with rates $(q_{n+j})_{j\ge0}=(\rho^nq_j)_{j\ge0}$, and its explosion time is $\zeta-\tau$. Multiplying all rates by $\rho^n$ divides all holding times by $\rho^n$. So $\zeta-\tau\overset d=\rho^{-n}\zeta=\bar\zeta/q_n$ conditionally, as claimed.
head: environment

label: cor:forecast
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:forecast}
On $\{t<\zeta\}$, with parameters known:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $\mathbb{E}[\zeta-t\mid\mathcal{F}_t]=m_t/(1-q)$ and $\operatorname{CV}(\zeta-t\mid\mathcal{F}_t)=\sqrt{(1-q)/(1+q)}$, whatever $t$ and whatever has happened so far;
\item every $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable forecast $\hat Z$ satisfies the conditional mean-squared-error bound
\[
\mathbb{E}[(\zeta-\hat Z)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_t]\ \ge\ \frac{1-q}{1+q}\,\big(\mathbb{E}[\zeta-t\mid\mathcal{F}_t]\big)^2 ,
\]
with equality at $\hat Z=\mathbb{E}[\zeta\mid\mathcal{F}_t]$;
\item if $[a,b]$ is an $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable interval with $\mathbb{P}(\zeta\in[a,b]\mid\mathcal{F}_t)\ge1-\delta$, then
\[
b-a\ \ge\ (1-\delta)(1-q)\,\mathbb{E}[\zeta-t\mid\mathcal{F}_t].
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: (a) follows from \cref{thm:selfsim,cor:moments}. (b) holds because $\mathbb{E}[(\zeta-\hat Z)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_t]=\operatorname{Var}(\zeta\mid\mathcal{F}_t)+(\mathbb{E}[\zeta\mid\mathcal{F}_t]-\hat Z)^2$. For (c), conditionally on $\mathcal{F}_t$ the variable $q_{N_t}(\zeta-t)$ has law $\Lambda_q$, whose density is bounded by $1$ (it is the convolution of the $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ density with another law). An interval carrying mass $1-\delta$ therefore has length at least $1-\delta$ in these units, and undoing the scaling with (a) gives (c). The bound in (c) is valid but generally not sharp; it does not identify the shortest predictive interval.
head: environment

label: rem:leadtime
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:leadtime}
Let $z_p$ be the $p$-quantile of $\Lambda_q$. By \cref{thm:selfsim}, $\mathbb{P}(\zeta-t\ge m_t z_p\mid\mathcal{F}_t)=1-p$ on $\{t<\zeta\}$. A response that needs lead time $\Delta$ and must be in place with probability at least $1-p$ therefore has to be launched while $m_t\ge\Delta/z_p$. For doubling-sized ideas at $\varepsilon=0.39$, $m_t$ is the current expected doubling time, $\mathbb{E}[\zeta-t\mid\mathcal{F}_t]=4.22\,m_t$, and the $5\%$ and $95\%$ quantiles are $z_{0.05}=2.148$ and $z_{0.95}=7.098$. A twelve-month response that must be in place with probability $0.95$ has to start while $m_t\ge12/z_{0.05}=5.59$ months. All of this is conditional on the model and its parameters being known.

label: prop:logperiodic
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:logperiodic}
In the lattice case with $\varepsilon>0$, the ideas arrive at $T_1,T_2,\dots$. Let $\nu:=\sum_{n\ge1}\delta_{\log(q_0(\zeta-T_n))}$ be the point process of their log-residual times, and let $\phi$ be the density of $\log\bar\zeta$. Then $\mathbb{E}\nu(\,\mathrm{d} x)=m(x)\,\mathrm{d} x$ with
\[
m(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\phi(x+n\ell),\qquad |m(x)-p(x)|\le\frac{e^{x}}{1-q},
\]
where $p$ is the $\ell$-periodic function
\[
p(x)=\frac1\ell\Big[1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\Re\Big(\Gamma\big(1-\tfrac{2\pi ik}{\ell}\big)\,e^{2\pi ikx/\ell}\Big)\Big],\qquad
\Big|\Gamma\big(1-\tfrac{2\pi ik}{\ell}\big)\Big|^2=\frac{2\pi^2k/\ell}{\sinh(2\pi^2k/\ell)} .
\]
In particular, as $x\to-\infty$ the relative amplitude of the fundamental harmonic of $\ell\,m(x)$ tends to $2|\Gamma(1+2\pi i/\ell)|\sim(4\pi/\sqrt\ell)\,e^{-\pi^2/\ell}$ as $\ell\to0$.
head: environment
name: Explosion-centred mean intensity

title: Proof
body_md:
From \eqref{eq:zeta}, $\zeta-T_n=q^n\zeta^{(n)}$ with $\zeta^{(n)}:=\sum_{j\ge0}e_{n+j}q^j/q_0\overset d=\zeta$. Hence $\log(q_0(\zeta-T_n))=-n\ell+\log\bar\zeta^{(n)}$, where each $\bar\zeta^{(n)}:=q_0\zeta^{(n)}$ has law $\Lambda_q$, and linearity of expectation gives $m$. The density of $\bar\zeta$ is bounded by $1$, so $\phi(y)=e^yf_{\bar\zeta}(e^y)\le e^y$, and
\[
|m(x)-p(x)|=\sum_{j\ge0}\phi(x-j\ell)\le e^x\sum_{j\ge0}q^j ,
\]
where $p(x):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\phi(x+n\ell)$. The periodisation $p$ of the integrable function $\phi$ has Fourier coefficients
\[
\frac1\ell\int_\mathbb{R}\phi(y)e^{-2\pi iky/\ell}\,\mathrm{d} y=\frac1\ell\,\mathbb{E}\big[\bar\zeta^{-2\pi ik/\ell}\big]=\frac1\ell\,\Gamma\big(1-\tfrac{2\pi ik}\ell\big)\frac{(q^{1-2\pi ik/\ell};q)_\infty}{(q;q)_\infty}=\frac1\ell\,\Gamma\big(1-\tfrac{2\pi ik}\ell\big),
\]
by \cref{thm:law}\ref{it:mellin} and the identity $q^{-2\pi ik/\ell}=e^{2\pi ik}=1$. The classical formula $|\Gamma(1+iy)|^2=\pi y/\sinh(\pi y)$ shows that the coefficients are absolutely summable. So the Fourier series converges uniformly to $p$, which is continuous because the periodisation converges locally uniformly. Stirling's formula gives the asymptotics.

label: prop:uncertain
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:uncertain}
In the lattice case with fixed $h$ and fixed current idea rate $q_0$, let $\varepsilon$ be random, independent of $(e_n)$, and suppose its law has a density $\pi$ on a neighbourhood of $0$ that is continuous at $0$ with $\pi(0)>0$. Then $\mathbb{E}[\zeta\mid\varepsilon>0]=\infty$ and
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}t\,\mathbb{P}(\zeta>t\mid\varepsilon>0)=\frac{\pi(0)}{q_0\log(1+h)\,\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon>0)} .
\]
Since $q_0\log(1+h)=g$ is the local log drift (\cref{box:calibration}, B), the constant equals $\pi(0)/(g\,\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon>0))$, which is also the limit of $t\,\mathbb{P}(T^\ast>t\mid\varepsilon>0)$ for the fluid waiting time $T^\ast=1/(\varepsilon g)$.
head: environment
name: Exact Pareto tail under parameter uncertainty

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $a:=\log(1+h)$, $C:=(q_0a)^{-1}$, and $\zeta_\varepsilon$ for the explosion time given $\varepsilon>0$. \emph{Infinite mean.} $\mathbb{E}\zeta_\varepsilon=1/(q_0(1-e^{-a\varepsilon}))\ge1/(q_0a\varepsilon)$, and $\int_0\pi(\varepsilon)\varepsilon^{-1}\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon=\infty$.

\emph{Large $\varepsilon$.} Chernoff's bound with $s=\frac12$ and the inequality $-\log(1-y/2)\le y$ on $[0,1]$ give $\mathbb{P}(\bar\zeta>x)\le e^{-x/2}\mathbb{E} e^{\bar\zeta/2}\le\exp\{-x/2+1/(1-q)\}$. Since $1/(1-q)\le1+1/(a\varepsilon)$, every $\varepsilon\ge4C/t$ satisfies $\mathbb{P}(\zeta_\varepsilon>t)\le e^{1-q_0t/4}$, uniformly. The contribution of $\{\varepsilon\ge4C/t\}$ to $t\,\mathbb{P}(\zeta>t,\varepsilon>0)$ is therefore at most $t\,e^{1-q_0t/4}\to0$.

\emph{Small $\varepsilon$.} For $t$ large, $4C/t$ lies in the neighbourhood where $\pi$ is a density, and the substitution $\varepsilon=u/t$ gives
\[
t\,\mathbb{P}(\zeta>t,\ 0<\varepsilon<4C/t)=\int_0^{4C}\pi(u/t)\,\mathbb{P}(\zeta_{u/t}>t)\,\mathrm{d} u .
\]
For fixed $u>0$, \cref{cor:moments} gives $\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{u/t}/t]=1/(q_0t(1-e^{-au/t}))\to C/u$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\zeta_{u/t}/t)=1/(q_0^2t^2(1-e^{-2au/t}))\to0$, so $\mathbb{P}(\zeta_{u/t}>t)\to\mathbf 1_{\{u<C\}}$ for $u\ne C$. The integrand is bounded, since $\pi$ is bounded near $0$ by continuity, so dominated convergence gives the limit $\int_0^{4C}\pi(0)\mathbf 1_{\{u<C\}}\,\mathrm{d} u=\pi(0)C$. Dividing by $\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon>0)$ proves the claim. The fluid statement is $\mathbb{P}(0<\varepsilon<1/(gt))\sim\pi(0)/(gt)$.

title: Theorem

\label{thm:detect}
\leavevmode

\item\label{it:det-lower} For all $\ell>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,\frac14)$: \quad $n^\ast(\alpha,\ell)\ \ge\ \big(6\log\tfrac1{4\alpha}\big)^{1/3}\,\ell^{-2/3}$.

head: environment
name: Cube-root law for the fixed-sample experiment

label: lem:logcosh
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:logcosh}
For $x\ge0$, $\tanh x\ge x/(1+x)$, and consequently $\log\cosh x\ge x^2/(2(1+x))$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $g(x):=(1+x)\tanh x-x$. Then $g(0)=0$ and $g'(x)=(1+x)\operatorname{sech}^2x-(1-\tanh x)=2\big((1+2x)e^{2x}-1\big)/(e^{2x}+1)^2\ge0$. Next let $f(x):=\log\cosh x-x^2/(2(1+x))$. Then $f(0)=0$ and $f'(x)=\tanh x-\frac{x(x+2)}{2(1+x)^2}\ge\frac{x}{1+x}-\frac{x(x+2)}{2(1+x)^2}=\frac{x^2}{2(1+x)^2}\ge0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The log-likelihood ratio is
\[
\mathcal L_n:=\log\frac{\,\mathrm{d} P_1^n}{\,\mathrm{d} P_0^n}=\sum_{k<n}\big(k\ell-(e^{k\ell}-1)q_0\tau_k\big).
\]
Under $P_0$, $q_0\tau_k=E_k$, and under $P_1$, $q_0\tau_k=e^{-k\ell}E_k$, with $(E_k)$ i.i.d.\ $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$.

\ref{it:det-lower} By the Bretagnolle--Huber inequality \cite{BH79}, \cite[Lemma~2.6]{Tsy09}, every test satisfies $P_0^n(\psi=1)+P_1^n(\psi=0)\ge\frac12\exp(-\mathrm{KL}(P_1^n\|P_0^n))$. Moreover
\[
\mathrm{KL}(P_1^n\|P_0^n)=\sum_{k<n}\big(k\ell-1+e^{-k\ell}\big)\le\frac{\ell^2}{2}\sum_{k<n}k^2<\frac{\ell^2n^3}{6}.
\]
If both errors are at most $\alpha$, then $2\alpha\ge\frac12e^{-\ell^2n^3/6}$, which rearranges to the claim.

\ref{it:det-upper} Take $\psi:=\mathbf 1\{\mathcal L_n>0\}$. By Markov's inequality, $P_0^n(\mathcal L_n>0)\le\mathbb{E}_0e^{\mathcal L_n/2}$ and $P_1^n(\mathcal L_n\le0)\le\mathbb{E}_1e^{-\mathcal L_n/2}$. Both equal the Bhattacharyya coefficient $\prod_{k<n}\int\sqrt{p_{0,k}p_{1,k}}$. For exponentials with rates $q_0$ and $q_0e^{k\ell}$ each factor is $2e^{k\ell/2}/(1+e^{k\ell})=\operatorname{sech}(k\ell/2)$. By \cref{lem:logcosh},
\[
-\sum_{k<n}\log\operatorname{sech}\frac{k\ell}{2}\ \ge\ \sum_{k<n}\frac{(k\ell/2)^2}{2(1+k\ell/2)}\ \ge\ \frac{\ell^2}{8(1+n\ell/2)}\sum_{k<n}k^2\ \ge\ \frac{\ell^2(n-1)^3}{24(1+n\ell/2)},
\]
using $\sum_{k<n}k^2=(n-1)n(2n-1)/6\ge(n-1)^3/3$.

\ref{it:det-sharp} \emph{Step 1: reduction to the likelihood-ratio test.} For $n\ge2$, $\mathcal L_n$ has a continuous law under both hypotheses, as a nondegenerate linear combination of independent exponentials. By the Neyman--Pearson lemma \cite{LR05}, for every test $\psi$ there is a threshold $t$ with $P_0(\mathcal L_n>t)=P_0(\psi=1)$ and $P_1(\mathcal L_n\le t)\le P_1(\psi=0)$. Hence $\mathrm{err}_n=\inf_t\max\{P_0(\mathcal L_n>t),P_1(\mathcal L_n\le t)\}$. Also $\mathrm{err}_n$ is nonincreasing in $n$, since a test may ignore data.

\emph{Step 2: Gaussian limit.} Fix $c>0$, let $n=n(\ell):=\lfloor c\ell^{-2/3}\rfloor$ and $\delta:=n\ell$, so $\delta\to0$ and $\ell^2n^3\to c^3$ as $\ell\downarrow 0$. For $x\ge0$, Taylor's theorem gives $\frac{x^2}2\le e^x-1-x\le\frac{x^2}{2}e^x$ and $\frac{x^2}{2}e^{-x}\le x-1+e^{-x}\le\frac{x^2}2$, and also $x\le e^x-1\le xe^x$ and $xe^{-x}\le 1-e^{-x}\le x$. With $S_2:=\sum_{k<n}(k\ell)^2\to c^3/3$, these give the following. Under $P_0$, $\mathbb{E}_0\mathcal L_n=-\sum_{k<n}(e^{k\ell}-1-k\ell)\in[-e^\delta S_2/2,-S_2/2]$ and $\operatorname{Var}_0\mathcal L_n=\sum_{k<n}(e^{k\ell}-1)^2\in[S_2,e^{2\delta}S_2]$. Under $P_1$, $\mathbb{E}_1\mathcal L_n=\sum_{k<n}(k\ell-1+e^{-k\ell})\in[e^{-\delta}S_2/2,S_2/2]$ and $\operatorname{Var}_1\mathcal L_n=\sum_{k<n}(1-e^{-k\ell})^2\in[e^{-2\delta}S_2,S_2]$. The Lyapunov ratio is at most $\mathbb{E}|E_1-1|^3e^{3\delta}\sum_{k<n}(k\ell)^3/(e^{-3\delta}S_2^{3/2})\le\mathbb{E}|E_1-1|^3e^{6\delta}\,\delta\,S_2^{-1/2}\to0$. By Lyapunov's central limit theorem, $\mathcal L_n\Rightarrow\mathcal N(\mp c^3/6,\,c^3/3)$ under $P_0$ and $P_1$ respectively.

\emph{Step 3: conclusion.} The limits are continuous, so by P\'olya's theorem the distribution functions converge uniformly, and therefore
\[
\mathrm{err}_{n(\ell)}(\ell)\to\inf_t\max\Big\{\bar\Phi\Big(\frac{t+\mu}{\sigma}\Big),\Phi\Big(\frac{t-\mu}{\sigma}\Big)\Big\}=\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu\sigma\Big)=\Phi\Big(-\frac{c^{3/2}}{\sqrt{12}}\Big),
\]
with $\mu=c^3/6$ and $\sigma^2=c^3/3$; the infimum is attained at $t=0$ by symmetry. Let $c^\ast:=(12z_\alpha^2)^{1/3}$. If $c<c^\ast$, the limit exceeds $\alpha$, so $\mathrm{err}_{n(\ell)}>\alpha$ for small $\ell$, and by monotonicity $n^\ast>c\ell^{-2/3}-1$. If $c>c^\ast$, the limit is below $\alpha$, so $n^\ast\le c\ell^{-2/3}$ for small $\ell$. Since $c$ was arbitrary, $\ell^{2/3}n^\ast\to c^\ast$.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:warning}
Under $H_1$, at the arrival time $T_n$ of the $n$-th idea, $\zeta-T_n$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{T_n}$ and distributed as $q^n\zeta$, where $q=e^{-\ell}$. Hence its quantiles are $q^n$ times the quantiles of $\zeta$, and

\[
\log W^\ast(\alpha,\ell)=-(12z_\alpha^2\,\ell)^{1/3}\,(1+o(1))\qquad(\ell\downarrow0).
\]

label: rem:unseparated
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:unseparated}
If $\ell$ is unknown and only $\ell>0$ is specified, no fixed-$n$ test has a nontrivial uniform error bound. Indeed $\mathrm{KL}(P_\ell^n\|P_0^n)=\sum_{k<n}(k\ell-1+e^{-k\ell})\to0$ as $\ell\downarrow0$, so $P_\ell^n\to P_0^n$ in total variation by Pinsker's inequality. If $P_0^n(\psi=1)\le\alpha$, then $P_\ell^n(\psi=1)\to P_0^n(\psi=1)\le\alpha$, and the worst-case type-II error over $\ell>0$ is at least $1-\alpha$. Meaningful formulations use a separated alternative $\ell\ge\ell_{\min}>0$, a local asymptotic power criterion, or a sequential design with an explicit criterion.
head: environment
name: No uniform fixed-sample test over unseparated alternatives

label: rem:baseline
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:baseline}
Suppose $\ell$ is specified but $q_0$ is unknown. The lower bound \ref{it:det-lower} still holds, since knowing $q_0$ can only help. The scale-invariant statistic $P_k:=\tau_k/\sum_{j<n}\tau_j$ removes $q_0$ exactly: integrating out $S=\sum_j\tau_j$ (Jacobian $S^{n-1}$) shows that $P$ is uniform on the simplex under $H_0$ and that, under rates $q_0e^{k\ell}$,
\[
\frac{f_\ell(P)}{f_0(P)}=\frac{\exp\{\ell\sum_{k<n}k\}}{\big(\sum_{k<n}e^{k\ell}P_k\big)^n}.
\]
The score at $\ell=0$ is $U_n=\sum_{k<n}k-n\sum_{k<n}kP_k$, whose null variance, by the Dirichlet covariance formula, is $\frac{n}{n+1}\sum_{k<n}(k-\bar k)^2\sim n^3/12$, against $\sum_kk^2\sim n^3/3$ for known $q_0$. This suggests the constant $(48z_\alpha^2)^{1/3}$, about $1.59$ times as many ideas. We have not proved this: it requires a composite minimax formulation, triangular-array limits under both hypotheses and a matching lower bound (\cref{sec:open}).

name: Unknown baseline: an invariant reduction

label: thm:lag
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:lag}
Let $\beta,\lambda,c,k,D>0$ and let $\varphi:[-D,0]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuous.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item In the deterministic delayed model \eqref{eq:lag}, there is a unique solution on $[-D,\infty)$; it is finite and increasing on $[0,\infty)$, so there is no finite-time blow-up, for any $r$.
\item If $r=\lambda/\beta>1$, then in the deterministic delayed model
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\log\log A(t)}{t}=\frac{\log r}{D}.
\]
\item With $D=0$ (and $r>1$) the solution blows up at $T^\ast=(\varepsilon ck^\lambda A(0)^\varepsilon)^{-1}$.
\item \emph{Stochastic delayed model.} Let ideas of size $h$ arrive at intensity $(c/h)k^\lambda A_{t-}^{-\beta}A_{t-D}^{\lambda}$, with $A_s=A_0$ for $s\le0$. Then the process does not explode: $N_t<\infty$ for all $t$, a.s.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Delayed feedback

label: eq:lagB
title: Proof
body_md:
Put $B:=A^\beta$ and $C:=\beta ck^\lambda$. Then \eqref{eq:lag} becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lagB}
\dot B(t)=C\,B(t-D)^{r}.
\end{equation}
The factor $A(t)^{1-\beta}$ has cancelled: diminishing returns at the frontier exactly offset the frontier's own growth.

(i) On $[jD,(j+1)D]$ the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:lagB} is a known continuous function, so $B$ is obtained by integration, step by step (the method of steps \cite{HVL93}). Conversely, any positive $C^1$ solution of \eqref{eq:lag} gives a solution of \eqref{eq:lagB}, which proves uniqueness. Since $\dot B>0$, $B$ is increasing on $[0,\infty)$, and $B(t)\ge B(0)+C(\min\varphi)^{\beta r}t\to\infty$.

(ii) \emph{Upper bound.} For $t\ge D$, $B(t+D)=B(t)+C\int_{t-D}^{t}B(v)^r\,\mathrm{d} v\le B(t)+CDB(t)^r$. Once $B\ge1$, this gives $\log B(t+D)\le r\log B(t)+\log(1+CD)$. So $u:=\log B+\log(1+CD)/(r-1)$ satisfies $u(t+D)\le ru(t)$, and therefore $\limsup t^{-1}\log\log B(t)\le(\log r)/D$.

\emph{Lower bound.} Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$. For $t\ge D$,
\[
B(t+D)\ \ge\ C\int_{t+D-\delta D}^{t+D}B(u-D)^r\,\mathrm{d} u\ \ge\ C\delta D\,B(t-\delta D)^r .
\]
So $v:=\log B+\log(C\delta D)/(r-1)$ satisfies $v(s+(1+\delta)D)\ge r\,v(s)$ for $s\ge D$. Since $B\to\infty$, $v$ is bounded below by some $v_{\min}>0$ on a window of length $(1+\delta)D$. Iterating gives $\liminf t^{-1}\log\log B(t)\ge(\log r)/((1+\delta)D)$, and we let $\delta\downarrow0$. Finally $\log\log A=\log\log B-\log\beta$.

(iii) This is \eqref{eq:ode} with $c$ replaced by $ck^\lambda$.

(iv) On $(jD,(j+1)D]$, $A_{t-}\ge A_{jD}$ and $A_{t-D}\le A_{jD}$. So the intensity is bounded by $Q_j:=(c/h)k^\lambda A_{jD}^{\lambda-\beta}$, which is $\mathcal{F}_{jD}$-measurable. By a thinning construction, conditionally on $\mathcal{F}_{jD}$ the number of ideas in that window is dominated by a Poisson variable with mean $Q_jD$, which is finite a.s.
